title: SSH Hardening and Secure Access
realWorldScenario: A small business has deployed a new Cisco ISR router as the network gateway. The network administrator needs to configure secure remote management access because the office location is remote and the team cannot always be on-site for console access. Unencrypted Telnet is currently the only option, exposing credentials to interception.
problemStatement: The router has no secure remote management configured. Administrators must use console access or unencrypted Telnet, which exposes credentials on the network.
businessImpact: Without secure remote access, administrators cannot manage the router remotely. This increases downtime during outages and exposes device credentials to potential interception, creating a security vulnerability.
objectives: Configure SSH version 2, generate cryptographic keys, create a local admin user, restrict VTY line access to SSH only, and verify secure remote connectivity.
learningObjectives: Understand why SSH is preferred over Telnet for remote management
Configure RSA cryptographic keys for SSH
Create local user accounts with secret passwords
Restrict VTY lines to SSH-only access
Verify SSH connectivity from a management PC
prerequisites: Basic IOS navigation (user mode, privileged mode)
Understanding of router physical interfaces
skills: Configure SSH version 2 on a Cisco router
Generate RSA keys for secure communication
Create local user accounts with privilege levels
Restrict VTY line access to SSH only
Test SSH connectivity from a management PC

steps.title: Inspect Current Router Configuration
steps.instruction: Before making any changes, examine the current router configuration. Run the following commands and note what remote access methods are currently configured: show running-config | section line vty, show ip ssh
steps.why: You need to understand the current state before making changes. This establishes a baseline and shows what remote access options exist.
steps.expectedOutput: No VTY lines configured for SSH. SSH not enabled.
hints: Look for "transport input" lines under VTY configuration
Check if RSA keys are generated

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping the inspection step
commonMistakes.solution: Always inspect current state before configuring

steps.completionCondition: Student has examined current VTY and SSH configuration

steps.title: Configure Hostname and Domain Name
steps.instruction: Enter global configuration mode and set the router hostname to R1 and domain name to secure-access.local. These values are required before generating SSH keys.
steps.why: SSH requires a hostname and domain name to generate unique RSA keys. Without these, the crypto key command will fail.
hints: The hostname should be set before generating keys
The domain name can be any valid DNS-style name

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to set domain name before generating keys
commonMistakes.solution: Set ip domain-name first, then generate RSA keys

steps.completionCondition: show running-config displays hostname R1 and ip domain-name secure-access.local

steps.title: Generate RSA Cryptographic Keys
steps.instruction: Generate RSA keys for SSH. Use the default key size (1024 bits is acceptable for lab purposes). The key generation process may take a moment.
steps.why: RSA keys are used for the SSH handshake. They encrypt the session and authenticate the router to connecting clients.
commands: crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 1024
hints: The modulus determines key strength. 1024 is minimum for labs.
You may see a prompt to overwrite existing keys - choose no if you want to keep existing keys

commonMistakes.mistake: Generating keys without setting hostname and domain first
commonMistakes.solution: Set hostname and domain-name before generating keys

steps.completionCondition: RSA keys are generated and show crypto key mypubkey rsa displays the public key

steps.title: Create Local Admin User
steps.instruction: Create a local user account named admin with privilege level 15 and secret password Admin123!. This account will be used for SSH authentication.
steps.why: Local user accounts provide authentication for VTY line access. The secret password is encrypted and stronger than a plaintext password.
hints: Use "secret" not "password" - secret is encrypted in the config
Privilege level 15 gives full administrative access

commonMistakes.mistake: Using "password" instead of "secret"
commonMistakes.solution: Always use "secret" for stronger encryption

steps.completionCondition: show running-config | include username displays the admin user

steps.title: Configure VTY Lines for SSH Only
steps.instruction: Configure VTY lines 0 through 4 to accept SSH connections only. Use login local for local database authentication. Disable Telnet access.
steps.why: Restricting VTY lines to SSH only prevents unencrypted Telnet sessions. This is a critical security hardening step.
steps.expectedOutput: VTY lines configured for SSH only.
hints: login local tells the router to check the local user database

commonMistakes.mistake: Using "transport input all" which allows both Telnet and SSH
commonMistakes.solution: Use "transport input ssh" to allow only SSH

steps.completionCondition: show running-config | section line vty shows transport input ssh and login local

steps.title: Enable SSH Version 2
steps.instruction: Explicitly enable SSH version 2, which is more secure than version 1. Version 2 uses stronger encryption and is the recommended standard.
steps.why: SSH version 1 has known vulnerabilities. Version 2 provides stronger encryption and is the current standard for secure remote access.
hints: You can verify SSH version with "show ip ssh"
Version 2 is the default on newer IOS versions, but it is good practice to explicitly configure it

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving SSH at version 1
commonMistakes.solution: Always configure ip ssh version 2

steps.completionCondition: show ip ssh displays SSH version 2 enabled

steps.title: Test SSH Connectivity
steps.instruction: From PC1, test SSH connectivity to R1 at 192.168.1.1. Use the admin username and Admin123! password. Verify that you can establish an SSH session.
steps.why: Testing confirms that SSH is working correctly and that the local user account can authenticate.
hints: The -l flag specifies the username for SSH
You will be prompted for the password: Admin123!

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to Telnet instead of SSH
commonMistakes.solution: Use ssh command, not telnet

steps.completionCondition: SSH session to R1 is established and user is at privileged prompt

commonErrors.symptoms: PC1 cannot establish SSH session to R1
troubleshootingSteps: 1. Verify RSA keys are generated (show crypto key mypubkey rsa)
2. Verify VTY lines have transport input ssh
3. Verify login local is configured on VTY lines
4. Verify the admin user account exists
5. Verify PC1 can reach R1 IP address
possibleCauses: VTY lines configured for Telnet only
IP connectivity issue between PC and router
commonErrors.fix: Generate RSA keys, configure VTY lines for SSH only, create local user account, verify IP connectivity
commonErrors.verificationAfterFix: SSH connection from PC1 to R1 succeeds

commonErrors.symptoms: SSH session starts but username/password is rejected
troubleshootingSteps: 1. Verify username spelling matches local database
2. Verify password is correct
3. Verify user privilege level allows VTY access
4. Check if local database is enabled (login local)
possibleCauses: User account not in local database
commonErrors.fix: Verify username and password, ensure user exists in local database with login local configured
commonErrors.verificationAfterFix: SSH authentication succeeds with correct credentials

finalVerification.successCriteria: SSH is enabled and accessible from the management workstation. RSA keys are generated, local user exists, VTY lines restrict to SSH only.
finalVerification.completionCriteria: Student can SSH from PC1 to R1 using the admin account and reach privileged EXEC mode.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is SSH preferred over Telnet for remote device management?
options: SSH encrypts all traffic including credentials, while Telnet sends everything in plaintext
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: SSH encrypts all traffic including credentials, while Telnet sends everything in plaintext
knowledgeCheck.explanation: SSH provides encrypted sessions, protecting credentials and data from interception. Telnet transmits all data, including passwords, in cleartext.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of RSA keys in SSH?
options: To compress data for faster transmission
To authenticate the server and encrypt the session
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: To authenticate the server and encrypt the session
knowledgeCheck.explanation: RSA keys are used during the SSH handshake to authenticate the server and establish an encrypted session.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which command creates a local user account with a secret password?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The "username" command creates a local user. "secret" encrypts the password in the configuration, making it more secure than plaintext "password".

title: VLAN Trunk Port Configuration
realWorldScenario: A small company is expanding its network to support two departments: Sales and Engineering. Each department needs its own broadcast domain (VLAN). The two switches are connected by a single uplink, and all inter-switch traffic must carry both VLANs without creating additional physical links.
problemStatement: Two switches are connected by a single cable, but only the native VLAN traffic passes. Sales and Engineering VLANs cannot communicate across the uplink.
businessImpact: Without trunking, adding a new VLAN requires additional physical cabling between switches. This increases cost, reduces scalability, and complicates network changes.
objectives: Configure a trunk port on two switches to carry multiple VLANs across a single uplink, verify trunk status, and test VLAN isolation.
learningObjectives: Understand the difference between access and trunk ports
Assign native VLAN on a trunk link
Restrict allowed VLANs on a trunk port
Verify trunk operation using show commands
prerequisites: Basic VLAN configuration (create VLANs, assign ports)
Understanding of broadcast domains
skills: Set native VLAN on trunk ports
Verify trunk status with show interfaces trunk

steps.title: Inspect Current Switch Configuration
steps.instruction: On both SW1 and SW2, examine the current port configuration. Run show interfaces switchport on the uplink port (Fa0/1) to see the current mode.
steps.why: You need to understand the current port mode before configuring trunking. By default, ports are in dynamic auto mode, which may not form a trunk.
steps.expectedOutput: Administrative Mode: dynamic auto, Operational Mode: static access
hints: The uplink port should show as access mode currently

commonMistakes.mistake: Configuring trunk without checking current mode
commonMistakes.solution: Always inspect current configuration first

steps.completionCondition: Student has examined current port mode on both switches

steps.title: Configure VLANs on Both Switches
steps.instruction: On both SW1 and SW2, create VLAN 10 (Sales) and VLAN 20 (Engineering). Name them appropriately.
steps.why: VLANs must exist on both switches before they can be carried over the trunk. Trunk ports forward traffic for all allowed VLANs, but the VLAN must be defined in the VLAN database.
hints: Create VLANs in global configuration mode
Use descriptive names for easier troubleshooting

commonMistakes.mistake: Creating VLANs on only one switch
commonMistakes.solution: VLANs must exist on both switches for trunking to work

steps.completionCondition: show vlan brief displays VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on both switches

steps.title: Configure Trunk Port on SW1
steps.instruction: On SW1, configure FastEthernet0/1 as a trunk port. Set encapsulation to dot1q, native VLAN to 99, and allowed VLANs to 10 and 20 only.
steps.why: Configuring the trunk port enables it to carry multiple VLANs. The native VLAN is untagged, and the allowed VLAN list restricts which VLANs traverse the trunk.
hints: The encapsulation command is required on some platforms
Native VLAN should be a dedicated VLAN, not a user VLAN

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting trunk encapsulation on older IOS
commonMistakes.solution: Use switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q

steps.completionCondition: show interfaces Fa0/1 switchport shows trunk mode with correct native VLAN and allowed VLANs

steps.title: Configure Trunk Port on SW2
steps.instruction: On SW2, configure FastEthernet0/1 as a trunk port with the same settings: dot1q encapsulation, native VLAN 99, allowed VLANs 10 and 20.
steps.why: Both ends of a trunk link must be configured as trunk ports. If only one side is a trunk, the link will not carry tagged frames correctly.
hints: Both sides must match for trunk to form
Use the same native VLAN on both sides

commonMistakes.mistake: Mismatched native VLAN on trunk ends
commonMistakes.solution: Native VLAN must match on both sides of the trunk

steps.completionCondition: show interfaces Fa0/1 switchport on SW2 shows trunk mode

steps.title: Verify Trunk Status
steps.instruction: On both switches, verify the trunk is operational. Run show interfaces trunk to see which VLANs are active on the trunk.
steps.why: Verification confirms that the trunk is carrying the expected VLANs and that the native VLAN is correctly configured.
hints: Look for the "Vlans allowed on trunk" line
Check that VLANs 10, 20, and 99 appear in the output

commonMistakes.mistake: Only checking one side of the trunk
commonMistakes.solution: Verify trunk status on both switches

steps.completionCondition: show interfaces trunk shows VLANs 10, 20, and 99 as allowed and active

steps.title: Configure Access Ports and Test VLAN Traffic
steps.instruction: On SW1, assign FastEthernet0/2 to VLAN 10. On SW2, assign FastEthernet0/2 to VLAN 20. Configure PC1 with IP 192.168.10.10/24 and PC2 with IP 192.168.20.10/24. Test connectivity within each VLAN.
steps.why: Access ports assign devices to specific VLANs. PCs in the same VLAN should be able to communicate directly through the switch.
hints: Access ports should be in access mode, not trunk
Each PC should be in a different VLAN

commonMistakes.mistake: Assigning access port to wrong VLAN
commonMistakes.solution: Double-check VLAN assignment matches the PC subnet

steps.completionCondition: PC1 and PC1 can ping within their respective VLANs

steps.title: Verify VLAN Isolation
steps.instruction: From PC1, attempt to ping PC2. The ping should fail because the PCs are in different VLANs and there is no router configured for inter-VLAN routing.
steps.why: VLANs provide broadcast isolation. Without a router or Layer 3 device, traffic cannot flow between VLANs.
hints: Inter-VLAN communication requires a router or Layer 3 switch

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting ping to succeed between VLANs
commonMistakes.solution: Different VLANs cannot communicate without a router

steps.completionCondition: Ping from PC1 to PC2 times out, confirming VLAN isolation

commonErrors.error: Trunk not forming - ports remain in access mode
commonErrors.symptoms: show interfaces trunk shows no trunk ports
troubleshootingSteps: 1. Verify both sides are configured as trunk (not dynamic auto)
2. Verify encapsulation matches (dot1q)
3. Verify native VLAN matches on both sides
4. Verify allowed VLANs overlap on both sides
commonErrors.fix: Configure both sides as trunk mode with matching encapsulation, native VLAN, and allowed VLANs
commonErrors.verificationAfterFix: show interfaces trunk shows both ports in trunking mode

commonErrors.error: Traffic from one VLAN appears on another VLAN
commonErrors.symptoms: PC in VLAN 10 can reach PC in VLAN 20 without router
troubleshootingSteps: 1. Check trunk allowed VLAN list
2. Verify access ports are assigned to correct VLANs
3. Check for VLAN leaks on trunk
possibleCauses: Trunk allowed VLANs include both VLANs when they should not
Access ports assigned to wrong VLAN
commonErrors.fix: Restrict trunk allowed VLANs, verify access port assignments
commonErrors.verificationAfterFix: Only intended VLAN traffic traverses the trunk

finalVerification.successCriteria: Trunk is operational on both switches, carrying VLANs 10 and 20. PCs in different VLANs are isolated.
finalVerification.completionCriteria: Student has configured trunk ports, verified VLAN traffic, and confirmed VLAN isolation.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary difference between an access port and a trunk port?
options: Access ports are faster than trunk ports
Access ports carry a single VLAN, while trunk ports carry multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tagging
Access ports require authentication, trunk ports do not
Access ports are only for routers, trunk ports are only for switches
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: Access ports carry a single VLAN, while trunk ports carry multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tagging
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Access ports connect end devices and carry traffic for one VLAN. Trunk ports connect switches and carry traffic for multiple VLANs using 802.1Q frame tagging.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of the native VLAN on a trunk port?
options: It is the default VLAN for all untagged frames
It is used for management traffic only
It encrypts traffic on the trunk
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: It is the default VLAN for all untagged frames
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The native VLAN is the VLAN whose frames are not tagged with 802.1Q headers on a trunk link. It is used for backward compatibility with devices that do not understand 802.1Q.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should you restrict allowed VLANs on a trunk port?
options: To reduce broadcast traffic and improve security by only allowing necessary VLANs
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: To reduce broadcast traffic and improve security by only allowing necessary VLANs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Restricting allowed VLANs prevents unnecessary broadcast traffic from crossing the trunk and limits exposure if an unauthorized device is connected.

title: Inter-VLAN Routing with Router
realWorldScenario: A small business has two departments: Sales (VLAN 10) and Engineering (VLAN 20). The company uses a single router with multiple physical interfaces to provide inter-VLAN routing. Recently, a new employee in Sales cannot reach the Engineering shared server. The network engineer must verify and restore inter-VLAN connectivity.
problemStatement: Two departments are on separate VLANs but cannot communicate. The router interfaces and switch VLAN configuration need to be verified and corrected.
businessImpact: Departmental isolation prevents collaboration. Sales cannot access Engineering resources, impacting cross-functional projects and reducing productivity.
objectives: Configure VLANs on a switch, assign access ports, configure router interfaces for each VLAN, and verify inter-VLAN connectivity.
learningObjectives: Understand why VLANs create separate broadcast domains
Configure VLANs on a Cisco switch
Assign switch ports to access VLANs
Configure router interfaces for inter-VLAN routing
Verify connectivity between VLANs using ping
prerequisites: Basic IP addressing and subnetting
Understanding of VLANs and broadcast domains
Basic switchport configuration
concepts: Ping as a connectivity verification tool
skills: Create and name VLANs on a switch
Configure router interfaces with IP addresses

steps.title: Inspect Current Network State
steps.instruction: On R1, SW1, PC1, and PC2, examine the current configuration. Check interface status, VLAN configuration, and IP addresses. Document what is missing.
steps.why: Understanding the current state helps identify what needs to be configured. You should see that interfaces are down, VLANs are not created, and IP addresses are not assigned.
steps.expectedOutput: Interfaces down, no VLANs configured, no IP addresses assigned.
hints: Look for interfaces showing "down" or "administratively down"
Check if VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 exist

commonMistakes.mistake: Not documenting current state before configuring
commonMistakes.solution: Always document baseline before making changes

steps.completionCondition: Student has examined and documented current network state

steps.title: Configure VLANs on the Switch
steps.instruction: On SW1, create VLAN 10 named Sales and VLAN 20 named Engineering. Verify with show vlan brief.
steps.why: VLANs must be created in the switch database before ports can be assigned to them. Each VLAN represents a separate broadcast domain.
hints: Create VLANs in global configuration mode
Verify with show vlan brief after creation

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to create VLANs before assigning ports
commonMistakes.solution: Create VLANs first, then assign ports

steps.completionCondition: show vlan brief shows VLAN 10 and VLAN 20

steps.title: Configure Access Ports for Each VLAN
steps.instruction: On SW1, assign FastEthernet0/2 to VLAN 10 and FastEthernet0/3 to VLAN 20. Set both ports to access mode.
steps.why: Access ports connect end devices to a specific VLAN. Each PC must be in the correct VLAN for its department.
hints: Use switchport mode access for end-device ports
Verify VLAN assignment with show interfaces switchport

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving ports in default VLAN 1
commonMistakes.solution: Explicitly assign access ports to the correct VLAN

steps.completionCondition: show interfaces switchport shows Fa0/2 in VLAN 10 and Fa0/3 in VLAN 20

steps.title: Configure Router Interfaces for VLANs
steps.instruction: On R1, configure GigabitEthernet0/0 with IP 192.168.10.1/24 and GigabitEthernet0/1 with IP 192.168.20.1/24. Bring both interfaces up with no shutdown.
steps.why: The router needs an IP address in each VLAN subnet to act as the default gateway. Each interface represents a different VLAN network.
steps.expectedOutput: Router interfaces configured with IP addresses.
hints: Each router interface connects to a different VLAN
The router IP becomes the default gateway for that VLAN

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the same IP subnet on both router interfaces
commonMistakes.solution: Each interface must be in a different subnet

steps.completionCondition: show ip interface brief shows both interfaces up with correct IP addresses

steps.title: Configure PC IP Addresses
steps.instruction: On PC1, set IP address to 192.168.10.10 with mask 255.255.255.0 and gateway 192.168.10.1. On PC2, set IP address to 192.168.20.10 with mask 255.255.255.0 and gateway 192.168.20.1.
steps.why: PCs need IP addresses in their respective VLAN subnets to communicate. The gateway is the router interface IP for that VLAN.
hints: The gateway should be the router interface IP for that VLAN
Both PCs should use the same subnet mask

commonMistakes.mistake: Using wrong default gateway
commonMistakes.solution: Gateway must be the router interface in the same subnet

steps.completionCondition: Both PCs have correct IP addresses and gateways

steps.title: Test Intra-VLAN Connectivity
steps.instruction: From PC1, ping the router VLAN 10 interface at 192.168.10.1. From PC2, ping the router VLAN 20 interface at 192.168.20.1. Verify local connectivity.
steps.why: Testing connectivity to the default gateway confirms that each PC can reach its local router interface. This is a prerequisite for inter-VLAN routing.
hints: If ping fails, check IP address, subnet mask, and cable

commonMistakes.mistake: Pinging the wrong router interface
commonMistakes.solution: Each PC should ping its own VLANs gateway

steps.completionCondition: PC1 can ping 192.168.10.1 and PC2 can ping 192.168.20.1

steps.title: Test Inter-VLAN Connectivity
steps.instruction: From PC1, ping PC2 at 192.168.20.10. From PC2, ping PC1 at 192.168.10.10. Verify that traffic routes through the router.
steps.why: Inter-VLAN ping confirms that the router is routing between VLANs. The router acts as the gateway for both networks.
hints: The router must have interfaces in both VLANs
Each PC must use the correct gateway
The router must have routing enabled (it is by default)

commonMistakes.mistake: Using wrong gateway on PC
commonMistakes.solution: Verify default gateway matches router interface in same subnet

steps.completionCondition: PC1 can ping PC2 and PC2 can ping PC1 across VLANs

steps.title: Verify Routing Table
steps.instruction: On R1, run show ip route to verify that directly connected routes exist for both VLAN subnets.
steps.why: The routing table should show directly connected routes for the subnets configured on the router interfaces. This confirms the router knows how to reach both networks.
steps.expectedOutput: C 192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, C 192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected
hints: Look for "C" entries which indicate directly connected routes
Each interface subnet should appear as a connected route

commonMistakes.mistake: Misconfiguring router interface IP addresses
commonMistakes.solution: Verify IP addresses are in the correct subnets

steps.completionCondition: show ip route displays connected routes for both VLAN subnets

commonErrors.symptoms: PC1 cannot ping PC2 across VLANs
troubleshootingSteps: 1. Verify router interfaces are up and have correct IPs
2. Verify PC IP addresses and gateways are correct
3. Verify switch ports are assigned to correct VLANs
4. Verify VLANs exist on the switch
5. Verify physical connections between router and switch
possibleCauses: Router interface down or no IP address
commonErrors.fix: Correct router interface configuration, verify PC gateways, verify VLAN assignments, ensure physical connectivity
commonErrors.verificationAfterFix: Inter-VLAN ping succeeds from PC1 to PC2

commonErrors.error: PC cannot ping its own gateway
troubleshootingSteps: 1. Verify router interface is up and has correct IP
2. Verify switch port is in correct VLAN
3. Verify PC has correct IP address and subnet mask
4. Verify cable is connected
possibleCauses: Wrong VLAN assignment on switch port
commonErrors.fix: Bring up router interface, correct VLAN assignment, configure correct PC IP, check cable
commonErrors.verificationAfterFix: PC can ping its default gateway

finalVerification.successCriteria: Router has interfaces in both VLAN subnets. PCs are in correct VLANs with correct gateways. Inter-VLAN ping succeeds.
finalVerification.completionCriteria: Student has configured VLANs, assigned ports, configured router interfaces, and verified bidirectional inter-VLAN connectivity.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why are VLANs necessary in a switched network?
options: To create separate broadcast domains and improve security
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: To create separate broadcast domains and improve security
knowledgeCheck.explanation: VLANs segment a physical network into multiple logical broadcast domains. This reduces broadcast traffic and improves security by isolating traffic between departments.

knowledgeCheck.question: In an inter-VLAN routing design using multiple router interfaces, what role does the router play?
options: It acts as a switch for VLAN traffic
It acts as the default gateway for each VLAN and routes between subnets
It assigns IP addresses to PCs
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: It acts as the default gateway for each VLAN and routes between subnets
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The router has an interface in each VLAN subnet. It routes traffic between these subnets, acting as the gateway for devices in each VLAN.

knowledgeCheck.question: What must be true for a PC in VLAN 10 to ping a PC in VLAN 20?
options: Both PCs must have the same IP address
The router must have interfaces in both VLANs, and PCs must use the router as their default gateway
The switch must have a trunk port to the router
Both PCs must be connected to the same switch port
knowledgeCheck.correctAnswer: The router must have interfaces in both VLANs, and PCs must use the router as their default gateway
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Inter-VLAN communication requires a Layer 3 device (router) with interfaces in each VLAN. PCs send traffic to their default gateway (the router), which routes it to the destination VLAN.
